blocks.text: Re: Engagement to perform a reserve adequacy review for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}
Dear Ms. Hudson:

This letter sets out the terms on which our firm will perform a reserve adequacy review for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}. It records what we will do, what we will rely on, and the basis on which we are engaged. We have written the terms plainly, because we would rather you know exactly what you are agreeing to than have to work it out later from the invoices. The work will begin on {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}}, and the paragraphs below cover the review itself, the people who will do it, the fee, and the standard terms that carry the engagement.
The Review and What It Covers

The purpose of the review is to form an opinion on whether the reserves carried by {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} are adequate to meet the obligations they are meant to fund, measured as of a valuation date we will fix with your staff at the outset. The opinion is the deliverable; everything else is in support of it. So there is no ambiguity about scope, the work has five parts.

items: A reconciliation of the reserve data you provide against your own financial records, so that the figures we test are the figures you carry.
A review of the assumptions underlying the current reserves, keeping the assumptions that regulation fixes separate from those that rest on judgment.
An independent estimate of the required reserves under the standards named below, developed from the data as reconciled rather than as received.
A comparison of that estimate against the carried reserves, with any difference attributed to its sources rather than reported as a single number.
A written report that states what the data show, what we assumed, and what we conclude, and keeps those three as three separate matters.

blocks.text: Matters outside this list are outside the engagement. We are not auditing your financial statements, setting your reserves for you, or opining on the adequacy of your rates. If you want any of those, we can scope them separately.
What We Will Need From You

The review turns on the data, so a few things on your side keep it on schedule. We will need the reserve detail, the financial records the reserves are carried against, and the assumption documentation in effect at the valuation date, and we will send a single itemized request rather than ask for these piecemeal. We also need one person we can put questions to as they come up, since a file usually raises a question that only your staff can settle. The sooner those requests are answered, the sooner we can reconcile against the right records the first time.
How We Will Work

We begin with your data and your own records, not with a template carried in from another client. Our reliance on the data is exactly that, reliance. We will test it for internal consistency and reconcile it to your records, but we do not audit it, and our opinion is conditioned on the data being complete and correct in the respects the report identifies. The review is performed in accordance with the applicable Actuarial Standards of Practice and the Code of Professional Conduct, and the report will name the standards it rests on. Where a figure reflects a judgment rather than a measurement, we will say so and give you the reasoning, rather than ask you to take the number on faith.
The Engagement Team

Jennifer Vasquez, a consulting actuary in our practice, owns the relationship and the day-to-day conduct of the work, and she is your point of contact for anything touching scope, schedule, or judgment. David Sherman, a senior analyst, builds and documents the valuation workbook and reconciles the data you send us. Megan Dudley, an actuarial associate, supports the exhibits and the data checks. I review the work and sign the opinion, and the professional responsibility for it is mine. You will hear from Jennifer Vasquez first, and she will coordinate the rest of us.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the review is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.fee}}, covering the work described above and the report that concludes it. We will invoice in three installments: a third at the start, a third on delivery of the draft report, and the balance on delivery of the final report. Invoices are due within thirty days. Out-of-pocket costs, if any, are billed at our cost and are expected to be minor. If anything arises that would materially change the fee, we will raise it with you in writing before the cost is incurred, not after.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins on the date noted above and runs until we deliver the final report, a period we expect to take about seven months. Either of us may end it on written notice. If you end it early, you owe us for the work performed to that point and for costs already committed. If we end it, we will give you enough notice and enough of our working files to let another actuary take up the work without repeating it.
Confidentiality

We will treat the information you give us as confidential and use it only for this engagement. We will not disclose it outside our firm except as you direct in writing or as the law requires, and where the law requires it we will tell you before we respond unless we are barred from doing so. Our working papers remain ours, and we hold them under the same duty of confidence.
Limitation of Liability

Our opinion is prepared for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} and for the use described in the report; it is not to be relied on by anyone else, or for any other purpose, without our written consent. Our liability to you arising out of this engagement, whether framed in contract or in negligence, is limited to the fee paid for the work, except for any liability that cannot be limited by law. We accept no liability to third parties.
Governing Law
This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our principal office sits, and any dispute arising under it belongs to the courts of that state.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign one copy of this letter where indicated below and return it to us, and keep the other for your file. Your signature is our authority to begin. If anything here reads differently from what we discussed, call me before you sign and we will fix the wording rather than paper over it.
Sincerely,
To: Jennifer Vasquez, Consulting Actuary; David Sherman, Senior Analyst
From: Megan Dudley, Actuarial Associate
Re: Reserve adequacy review for {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}}: where we are starting

The engagement is open as of {{fact:f:E-2017-001.start}}, and I wanted to put down in one place what we are setting out to do, so that we are all working from the same picture through these first weeks. The object of the review is a defensible opinion on whether the reserves {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} carries are adequate for the obligations behind them. Everything we do over the next several months is in service of that one question, and it helps to keep it in view while the work is still mostly setup.

The first thing in front of us is the data. David Sherman will take the reserve files as they arrive and reconcile them against the client's own records before any of it feeds an exhibit, and he will write down what he is relying on rather than carry it in his head. Nothing gets built on a figure we have not tied out. If something in the files looks off, we flag it early and in writing, because a question raised now is far cheaper than a correction discovered later in the report.

Alongside that, we start pulling apart the assumptions behind the current reserves, keeping the ones that regulation fixes separate from the ones that rest on judgment, since those turn into two different conversations by the end. Jennifer Vasquez will steer the judgment calls and decide which of the client's questions the data can actually answer and which it cannot, and I will keep the working assumptions documented as we go, so the report can show plainly what we measured and what we assumed. Those are the two columns that keep an opinion like this honest, and it is easier to keep them apart from the start than to separate them afterward.

Our point of contact at the client is Michelle Hudson, their Director of Operations, and the data requests run through her. I will keep a simple log of what we have asked for, what has arrived, and what is still outstanding, and I will circulate it so none of us has to guess where a file is. Anything that touches scope or fee goes back to Jennifer Vasquez rather than out from us directly, so the client hears one voice on those questions and not three.

A word on how the review reads when it is done, because it shapes how we work now. The report will separate what the data show from what we assumed and from what we conclude, and it will name the Actuarial Standards of Practice it rests on. That structure is easier to build into the workpapers from the first week than to impose at the end, so as we go, please tag anything that is a judgment as a judgment and anything that is measured as measured. On timing, we have about seven months, and the front of that is the reconciliation; the analysis and the writing only move as fast as the data lets them, which is another reason to get the request out clean and early.

For this week, the one thing I need from each of us is our part of the initial data request for Michelle Hudson, so we can send it as a single list rather than in pieces. Send me your items by Thursday and I will assemble the request for Jennifer Vasquez to review before it goes out.
Hello Michelle,

I am opening this thread so our notes on the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} reserve adequacy review stay together in one place as the work gets going. For the file, the contacts are set: on your side, Michelle Hudson, Director of Operations, as our point of contact for the data; and on ours, Jennifer Vasquez, who leads the engagement and is the person to come to on scope or judgment, and David Sherman, who reconciles the reserve files as they arrive.

We have made a start on the setup, and nothing here needs anything from you today; I mostly want you looking at the same picture we are. The one thing that will move us forward is the reserve data itself. Over the next few days we will send a single, itemized request rather than a trickle of small ones, so you and your team can pull it in one pass.

Once you have that list, the most useful next step would be a short call to walk through anything on it that is ambiguous at your end, so we reconcile against the right records the first time. I will send the request shortly and suggest a couple of times.
Best
Good morning Michelle,
Short version: I can start the reconciliation as soon as I have three files, and one figure in what you have already sent does not tie out, so I want to settle it before it reaches an exhibit.
The three files I need are these.

items: The reserve detail behind the summary you sent, at the seriatim or grouped level, whichever your system produces.
The year-end financial figures the reserves are carried at, so I can reconcile to your own records rather than to a total.
The assumption set {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} had in effect at the valuation date, in whatever form it was documented.

blocks.text: The line that does not tie is the aggregate reserve on the summary tab; it sits a little above the sum of the detail beneath it. It is most likely a grouping or rounding difference, but I will not carry it forward until I know which. For the working papers I am logging each file against the request and the date it arrives, and the request is addressed to you, Michelle Hudson, so please route the files back to me and copy Megan Dudley, who keeps our running log. Anything on scope, or on the shape of the opinion, is Jennifer Vasquez's call rather than mine.
Best
Hello Michelle,

Thank you, and please do not feel you have to send everything at once. To keep it simple on your side, I have pulled it all into the single request I promised, so you are working from one list instead of several. It covers the reserve detail, the year-end figures David Sherman will reconcile against your records, and the assumption documentation for the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} valuation. For our file I have you, Michelle Hudson, down as the one contact for the data, so sending it to me is enough and you need not copy the whole team.

On the single line David flagged, I would not read anything into it yet. Differences of that kind are ordinary this early, and surfacing it now is exactly what we want, rather than finding it later in a footnote. If it turns out to be a real difference, Jennifer Vasquez will walk it through with you before any of us draws a conclusion from it, though I do not expect it to come to that.

If it is easiest, send whatever is ready first and the rest as it comes; I will confirm each piece as it lands so you always know where things stand. The one item that helps most this week is the reserve detail, since that is what frees David Sherman to begin.
Best
Good morning Michelle,
To save a round trip: when you pull the reserve detail, two things about the format will let it reconcile on the first pass rather than the second.

items: Please export it at the same grouping level as your year-end financial figures, so the two tie to each other directly. If the systems group differently, a key that maps one to the other is enough and I can do the rest.
Include the valuation-date totals as your system reports them, unrounded, so the small difference I flagged earlier resolves cleanly against the source.

blocks.text: That is all I need to close out the open line and start the substantive work on the {{fact:f:E-2017-001.client}} reserves. Megan Dudley keeps the running log, so a copy to her when you send keeps our record straight; and if any of this touches how the question is framed rather than how it is measured, that is Jennifer Vasquez's call. I will note the tie-out in the working papers under your name, Michelle Hudson, so our reliance on the file is documented.
Best
